analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Submitted. We'll hear arguments next in Seller Tax Corporation against Contrat. Thank you. Mr. Van Korten, I think you may proceed whenever you're ready. Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. This case is here under writ of certiorari to the District of Columbia Circuit, which, in a decision written by Judge Starr, reversed the summary judgment granted by Judge Ritchie of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia. Judge Bork descended from that decision and held that the decision should have been affirmed. The chronology of this case in the District Court, I think, is quite important. The case was filed in September 1980. There were some preliminary, rather abortive efforts at discovery, but the first discovery, which is truly relevant to this proceeding, was propounded in February 1981, which was a joint defense set of interrogatories, 52 in number, numbers 51 and 52 of which asked very specific questions about product exposure and asked very specific questions about witnesses who would testify to product exposure. That joint defense set of interrogatories was not answered until June 1981. However, when they were finally answered, the interrogatories 51 and 52 were simply answered by saying that those answers will be supplemented at a later date. The defense filed a motion to compel timely in July. The answers were not supplemented. There was never an order on the motion to compel. The answers were not supplemented until February 1982, after Celotex had filed a motion for summary judgment, which is the subject of this appeal. The supplementary answers still did not refer to any exposure to Celotex products. Interrogatories 51 and 52, as a matter of fact, were not supplemented at all. Celotex had previously made a motion for summary judgment in September, which was withdrawn. Celotex renewed its motion in December. The fact that the trial judge would seriously be considering motions for summary judgment based upon the lack of product identification cannot possibly have been a surprise to plaintiff's trial counsel, since the district court judge had already granted a number of such motions. However, the motion was pending from December 1981 until July 1982, when the judge finally ruled. There has been a lot of attention given in respondent's brief to whether the motion went only to exposure to Celotex products in the District of Columbia or to exposure anywhere. I would submit that although the language of the motion may not have been a model of clarity, the statement of undisputed facts certainly indicated that there was no evidence of exposure to Celotex products either in the District of Columbia or anywhere else. That certainly was the view of the majority in the Court of Appeals. It was the view of all three of the members of the Court of Appeals, and it was the view of the district judge as well, since he said that there was no admissible evidence of exposure in the District of Columbia or elsewhere. Well, was there any admissible evidence of exposure anywhere else? There was testimony of the decedent at his workman's comp proceeding, which was a proceeding at which Celotex was not a party and which counsel for respondent concede at this point is inadmissible for any purpose. How about that letter from Mr.—was it Mr. Hoff? The letter from Mr. Hoff, Your Honor, certainly did not purport to be made on personal knowledge. It was not under oath. It also, I think, from reading the letter pretty clearly indicates that it was not on personal knowledge. He refers to what we understand and our understanding repeatedly. Mr. Hoff was an assistant corporate secretary of corporation with offices all over the United States. Let's suppose that Mr. Hoff, he was out of state, I guess. He was in Illinois, was he? Or was he? That's correct, Justice White. I suppose that his letter was unambiguous, that he knew that from personal knowledge that this man had been exposed to asbestos. And there he was. And you knew the plaintiff had at some point in this case had told you, had mentioned this letter, I take it. So you knew about the letter? The first time that the letter was produced was in response to Sellotex's first motion for summary judgment. Right, right. So you knew about it when you finally made your second motion. That's correct. Sellotex's trial counsel did. And suppose that, suppose the plaintiff had said, we're going to call Mr. Hoff. Well, the plaintiff had said that, Justice White. The point that I think is important to focus upon is that we only reach that question, if Sellotex is correct, on the first issue in this case, and on the issue that's really the reason that the petition for cert was filed, which is the holding of the majority below that the plaintiff need have produced nothing. The plaintiff could have simply sat silent because Sellotex did not affirmatively produce evidence of no liability. The majority below expressly said that Sellotex, that it was not sufficient to point to the fact that plaintiff had not indicated that there was any admissible evidence of liability, that Sellotex had to show that the plaintiff could not produce any admissible evidence of liability. That burden is a burden which it would be impossible for Sellotex to meet, because let's say that Sellotex went back and prevailed upon the problems with Mr. Hoff's letter. There would be no way to renew the motion because even if Mr. Hoff was clearly mistaken, Sellotex could not possibly file a motion saying that there was never any other exposure at any other point in the decedent's life. It seems to me that it might be just a question if his letter really was a meaningful letter, was unambiguous. It might be just a question of who had to go take his deposition. That may be correct, Justice White. Who do you think would have to, if this letter was a straightforward letter that really did give some credence to the plaintiff's case, do you think to make your motion you think you would have to go take his deposition? Had I been trial counsel for Sellotex, if the letter indicated that Mr. Hoff really knew something, I would have certainly been there taking the deposition in Chicago in any event. The majority in the Court of Appeals expressly refused to pass on the admissibility of the evidence, did they? That's correct, Justice Ramirez. They referred to it, they discussed it, but they did expressly refuse to pass. They said some of it, it was partially curable. That's correct. I don't think that that's at all clear from the record. And I would point out that counsel for Sellotex, an argument on the motion for summary judgment, specifically called the Court's attention to the inadmissibility of the letter to the fact that it was not under oath, and as a matter of fact, Mr. Hoff, since his company had paid workman's compensation benefits, may have indeed had a subrogation interest in the case, although that was not of record. I think it's interesting, though, that trial counsel for the plaintiffs didn't request additional time to put this evidence in admissible form, and even after the district court had granted the motion for summary judgment and had thrown the plaintiff out of court against Sellotex, never filed a motion for reconsideration with an affidavit showing that Mr. Hoff really, in fact, knew anything about the facts of this case. Mr. Van Coten, certainly the language in this Court's opinion in a Dickies v. Crescent company cuts against your argument, doesn't it? There are a couple of sentences of language that I believe, in fact, do, Justice O'Connor. However, I think that if you read what the state of the factual record was before this Court in a Dickies, the holding of this Court does not cut against our position. That was the position taken by the Fifth Circuit in Fontenot, which we cited in our reply brief, and it was the position taken by the Third Circuit in the Inre Japanese Electronics Products case, which this Court just cited last week under the name of Matsushita Electronic. I would point out that if the opinion of the majority in the D.C. Circuit was correct, I don't believe that from the state of the record in the Inre Japanese Electronics Products case, if that case would have ever even been before the Court, because at the trial court level and at the appellate court level, counsel for the plaintiff in that case strenuously argued exactly what counsel for respondents are arguing in this case, namely that the trial court was incorrectly placing the burden upon the plaintiffs to show that they had some admissible evidence with which to support their claim and that the defendants had not affirmatively negated the possibility that plaintiffs could prove their claim. The Third Circuit in that case discussed in some detail its view of the actual holding of this Court in a Dickies and came to the conclusion that the real question was not the question of who had the initial burden of producing evidence on a motion for summary judgment, at least when a motion for summary judgment was made by the party who would not have the burden of proof at trial, but that the real question is whether looking at all of the evidence in totality, the Court is persuaded that there is not, in fact, a genuine dispute of material fact. And in the opinion of the Third Circuit in that case, in the opinion of the Fifth Circuit in Fontenot, decided within the last couple of months it's appropriate to consider who will have the burden of proof at trial. And I would submit, in fact, that reading what the record was before this Court in a Dickies, that there was ample circumstantial evidence with which to support the plaintiff's claim. The real complaint, I believe, of the defense there was that there was no direct evidence. May I ask you to comment on one thing that I'm a little puzzled about? The motion, as I read it, directs the Court's attention to proximate cause as a result of distribution within the jurisdictional limits of the District Court. And then in your memorandum in support, the record is totally devoid of any such evidence within the jurisdictional confines of this Court. I get the impression the motion was intended to say that if there wasn't anything tying the case to this particular federal district, that you would prevail. Is that a correct reading of your motion? Well, I wasn't trial counsel for Sellotex, and my firm wasn't, Justice Stevens, so I can't say for sure. However, the statement of material facts which are not in dispute goes substantially further than that, I believe. But it ends at the last sentence on that, on Joint Defendants 172, ends with the words within the jurisdictional limits of this Court. So that seems to be consistent with the notion. But it, well, I believe Justice Stevens is phrased in the alternative. It says there is no evidence whatsoever that the decedent was ever exposed to any product containing asbestos designed, manufactured, or distributed by Sellotex Corporation, or that any such product was in any way the proximate cause of the decedent's death within the jurisdictional limits of the Court. I'm not sure, frankly, what the last part of that sentence means, but it's clearly stated in the alternative. See, I was wondering if, although they didn't put inadmissible evidence in response, if they said, well, we're going to try to prove our case by evidence of what happened elsewhere, and therefore the motion's legally insufficient, and the district judge disagreed. That's not a... Justice Stevens, I'm not sure, but it's also well settled that a district judge may grant a motion for summary judgment upon grounds other than those cited in the motion. And two cases to that effect are Broderick Wood Products versus U.S. 195, Fed Second 433, and Board of National Emissions versus Smith, 182, Fed Second 362. Those are Tenth and Seventh Circuit cases. And I believe Wright and Miller also agree. The question is whether the district judge, in viewing the entire record, believes that summary judgment is appropriate. And so even if you're correct, Justice Stevens, in what perhaps all Texas Trial Council meant with that language, I don't think that there's any authority that that would remove the discretion of the district court to grant summary judgment if it viewed it as appropriate. Again... Mr. Van Corden, you say the discretion of the district court to grant summary judgment. It's my understanding this question of summary judgment raises the question of law, and that it isn't reviewed, well, the district court might have gone either way appropriately, the same way you review kind of equitable decisions by the district court. That's clearly correct, Justice Rehnquist, in a situation where the district court incorrectly grants a motion for summary judgment. I believe that where the district court, in its discretion, denies the motion that the law may be otherwise. Well, you can't appeal from a denial. Certainly not an immediate appeal. That's correct. So you don't have much case law. Well, that's correct. But that's the point, that it's indeed discretionary to that extent. But the point, I think, is that the district judge, and I think it's interesting that in their brief, respondents concede that had Judge Ritchie set up a formal discovery schedule and had the time for discovery stated in that formal schedule ended, that at that point, if the plaintiffs had not produced admissible evidence of exposure to Sellotex products, that the district court could have granted a motion for summary judgment on that basis. In this case, there never was a formal order entered stating when discovery must cease. A number of judges in the district court for the District of Columbia, at any rate, don't typically enter that type of an order. It wasn't entered, but Judge Ritchie had made it very clear in ruling on previous summary judgment motions that he thought that the time to try to come up with some kind of admissible evidence to keep individual defendants in the case was rapidly disappearing. Yes, but is that a fair sign? I'm just reading the colloquy before he ruled when they produced the Huff letter. He didn't reject that because it was inadmissible. He said, let me see the Huff letter. Where does it say it was done in the District of Columbia? I did not say in the District of Columbia. It had no contract with the District. For that reason, he refused to rely on it, as I understand it. So he was, maybe I misread it, but he seemed to be focusing on that issue. And be concerned with the locality of the exposure. And later on, they, in effect, represented they could prove exposure in other areas. And he, in effect, said, I don't care about other areas. Well, that is certainly a possible way, Justice Stevens, of reading that colloquy. If the only holding of the D.C. Circuit had been that it was troubled about that and wanted a more fully developed factual record because of that, we wouldn't be here. The reason that we're here is for you. Well, if he thought that was a legal, essential element of the plaintiff's claim, exposure in the District, he wouldn't have asked for further discovery because the plaintiff said, we can't get you anything on that point. So he would just dismiss the case. And you don't contend that that would make the case deficient, as I understand you? I don't contend, certainly, that it would make for a ruling on the merits, as was entered in this case. The, again, the crux of our case is that the opinion of the majority below, in holding that simply pointing to the failure of the party with the burden of proof at trial to produce any indication of discovery that they have admissible evidence, makes... If he had obtained an affidavit from Hoff, for example, and he stated it on his own knowledge that there was exposure in Illinois, that would have satisfied the plaintiff's requirement, in your view, I suppose. I think that's correct. If Mr. Hoff had stated that there was exposure to cell tax products, and that's another issue that was not briefed and argued in the District Court, but I think it's quite clear that plaintiffs could not possibly prevail upon exposure to carry Canadian asbestos products. In any event, were they able to prove such exposure, and I think that the record in this case falls woefully short of showing that they could, in fact, produce evidence of exposure to those products. The rule that has been urged by pretty much unanimously the academic commentators and has been held by the Fifth Circuit in Fontenot and Third Circuit in In-Ray Japanese Electronics Products, which would harmonize the burden on the motion for summary judgment with the burden at trial, is a rule which will have salutary effects in permitting trial courts to narrow down the issues in the case to what are, in fact, the real issues. And my firm, on occasion, represents plaintiffs as well as defendants. There are instances where I've seen where a defense counsel will raise affirmative defenses, for example, of a decedent's contributory negligence, without any evidence produced in the course of discovery that the plaintiff's decedent was contributory negligent. The rule that we're urging would not be a rule that would just help defendants. It would help trial courts, in that instance, narrow down the real focus of the case to what were the real issues which were supported by the real evidence in the case. I think that that is the importance of this case. My office has been involved in over 1,000 asbestos cases in Maryland and the District of Columbia. It's, by definition, impossible to prove, for a defendant to prove, that the plaintiff cannot possibly produce evidence of exposure or proximate causation. The best that the defense can ever do in any of these cases is say that simply at this point, the plaintiff has not done so. And that's true in many other respects, in many products liability cases and other cases as well. So the holding that we would urge would allow trial judges to control their dockets, to get rid of frivolous cases before putting not only the parties but the judicial system to the burden of a needless trial, and to whittle the issues down to what are, in fact, the real issues in the cases. As we discuss, the holdings of the lower courts are unanimous. The motion for summary judgment, at least if you reach the issue of the respondent's evidence, can only be opposed with what would, in fact, be admissible evidence at trial. We've cited those cases in our brief, and they aren't really disputed. The question, really, as was pointed out by the District Court, is whether they even need to get to that question, whether the plaintiff had to produce anything or whether the plaintiff, in response to Saltax's motion, could have stood there, filed nothing, said nothing, and still obtained a reversal. That was the holding of the majority below, and we would submit that there's nothing, in this Court's opinions, in a Dickey's or any other case which requires such a holding, and that such a holding largely eliminates the utility of Rule 56 in a great variety of cases. If I could, I'd like to reserve the rest of my time for rebuttal. Thank you. Mr. Smith. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. Our position in this case is a simple one. When Saltax moved for summary judgment, it relied solely on the state of the record as it then stood in the case. Such a motion is, we submit, perfectly appropriate, where the record does show that the plaintiff lacks sufficient evidence for trial. But here the record showed precisely the opposite. It showed that the plaintiff had two pieces of evidence ready to use at trial. She had a witness, and she had sales records supplied by Saltax, which corroborated that witness's specific allegations. Now... But that's not the ground that the Court of Appeals went on, Mr. Smith. Your Honor, the Court of Appeals ruling was that the motion was unsupported, and therefore there was no obligation on the part of the plaintiff to come back with any sort of affidavits to substantiate her case. And that is essentially the point I'm making here as well. The motion was unsupported because, although these two types of trial evidence were listed by the plaintiff, the defendant, Saltax, did nothing in its motion to contest or discredit those two types of evidence in any way. Well, but the Court of Appeals says at page 5A of the petition, we need not, however, reach the evidentiary issue inasmuch as the defendant's moving papers were patently defective on their face. I read the majority opinion, and I think it's hard to read it otherwise, as saying that we don't have to worry about whether the plaintiffs made any showing at all because it was the defendants who had to make a showing, and they did not make this negative showing. Yes, they had to make a showing, but I think I want to clarify one point. They didn't have to make a showing of affirmative evidence that they were not liable on the tort. What they had to do in a case like this, and it's fair to expect them to do it, is they had to take the evidence that was listed by the plaintiff in her interrogatory response and in some way show that the plaintiff's trial case would not be sufficient once the case went to trial. That is the kind of support that a defendant manufacturer in this kind of case has to offer before it can move for summary judgment. Where do you find that language in the Court of Appeals' opinion that supports what you just said? Well, Your Honor, I think the Court of Appeals' opinion is somewhat vague on what kind of support you have to offer before your motion is valid, but they were quite clear that you didn't have to offer an affidavit, and they said several times we're not going to tell you exactly what sort of support you have to offer. But the law is quite clear that you have two choices when you move for summary judgment. Either you can produce affirmative evidence to show that you're not liable, or you can just ask the plaintiff to preview his trial case, and when he does so, you can then try to show that that trial case won't do the job. And having done that, you still don't have to come up with affirmative evidence. That's enough. What if the defendant moves for a summary judgment in a case like this, and the plaintiff says we don't have to prove anything, because under the Court of Appeals' ruling here, it's up to the defendant to show that the plaintiff has never been exposed to asbestos. Let me try to deal with this. I think it's clear that, and this rule survives the Court of Appeals' decision, that every plaintiff in every case has a duty to identify evidence that he plans to use at trial. That will generally occur in an interrogatory response before the motion is even filed. If the plaintiff totally fails to identify evidence that he plans to use at trial, and discovery has gone on for a long time and is closed, at that point, his failure to identify evidence is itself support for the defendant's summary judgment motion. Well, that sounds like a sensible rule, but I just didn't see the Court of Appeals as even mentioning a rule like that. Well, Your Honor, I think, you know, it may be that the Court of Appeals' ruling needs to be clarified in this Court, but I see nothing there that says that you have to have affirmative evidence. Do you agree that the standard for granting summary judgment is basically the same as whether a motion for directed verdict should be granted? In the sense that you look at the burden of proof in the defendant, certainly that should be taken into account. Well, you say it should be taken into account. What does that mean? Well, there's one key difference between the two situations. At summary judgment, the plaintiff's evidence has never been presented. The witnesses have yet to testify, and so the defendant can't just stand up at the end of the process and say, I think this is insufficient. At the summary judgment stage, the defendant has to do something affirmative to undermine the plaintiff's listed evidence. If she says she has a witness, the defendant has to take the deposition. Do you disagree with that word admissible? You must. You're just going to list some evidence, you say. Does it have to be admissible evidence? Well, I think, Your Honor, if the evidence you list for trial is three inadmissible documents and you concede that that's all you have for trial, then that's a valid basis for some of the judge. What did you list in this case that you think satisfied your obligation? The interrogatory responses listed a witness with direct knowledge of the facts, Mr. Hoff. How do you, what did it, you listed him and you said what about him? The interrogatory that asked him to, asked for him to be, for witnesses, the one that he was listed for specifically said, do you have a person with knowledge of the relevant facts? And he was listed. I would add that there's nothing in his letter that even suggests that he doesn't lack, that he doesn't have requisite knowledge. All of this stuff about our understanding and everything was only in that portion of the letter that goes to which company, which corporation manufactured the product. And you suggest that your obligation, if you had any, was just to list a witness, and you don't need to get an affidavit from him and present it in opposition to any motion, and you don't need to take his deposition. What this case is about is when a party opposing summary judgment incurs that further duty, not just to list a witness, but to present an affidavit from that witness. And the rule is clear that you have that further duty only where the motion itself is supported in some way other than by the lawyer's mere assertions. Here, the motion was essentially unsupported because it relied entirely on the existing record, and that record, those interrogatory responses, didn't by any means suggest that the plaintiff lacked a meritorious case, indeed quite the contrary. So the motion was invalid on its face, and under our system, at that point, the party opposing summary judgment... So you think once you listed that witness, if the defendant was going to move for summary judgment, it had to deal with Mr. Hawke? That's exactly right, Justice White. They had to do that because they had to provide some... Either go take his deposition or present an affidavit or... There's a number of things they could do. They could depose him, they could get an affidavit from someone else saying he was never there at the time, or they could, in some other way, deny the claim. Obviously, if the defendant has the capacity just to deny the claim on his own, that's enough to carry the initial burden at the summary judgment stage as well. But here, Celotex never took any of these steps. Now, I think it's useful to review a few more of the factual events in the district court because they help to show why it really is hard to understand the failure of Celotex to do anything else in this case to support its motion. First, well before the motion was filed, the plaintiff did tell Celotex every fact that she planned to prove at trial to establish the liability of Celotex. She told Celotex the time and place of the alleged exposure, the particular product involved, and the name of the person, Mr. Hoth, who had direct knowledge of all of these events. She did all this in her response to the earlier summary judgment motion, which was later withdrawn by Celotex. And that response included both the deposition transcript of the decedent and the Hoth letter. The Hoth letter and the deposition transcript both described the same set of exposures during 1971 when the decedent was working for Anning Johnson, a company in Chicago. Now, from this point on, I think it's important to recognize, everyone in the case proceeded with these specific allegations in mind. Celotex investigated the allegations and came up with these sales records which conformed exactly to the story that had been told by the decedent and Hoth. It then filed for a change of venue, filing these sales records in support of its own motion, and said the reason we should move to Chicago is because this case is all about these Anning Johnson exposures. Then, nine days later, we got this summary judgment motion. And that motion, peculiarly enough, doesn't say anything at all about the Anning Johnson exposures. It simply denies that there's evidence of exposures in Washington, D.C. Could you direct me to your interrogatory answer where you mentioned Mr. Hoth? That's on page 202.01, Your Honor. Do you think you have to at least say what Mr. Hoth, what your witness will testify to? I think that's certainly something that the defendant has a right to know. Here, they had his letter for at least three or four months before this interrogatory response was filed. And they had had the time before this was filed to investigate the claim fully, produce these sales records, and they knew exactly what Mr. Hoth was going to say. The reason that this wasn't all set out in more detail in the interrogatory responses probably was that they thought the information had already been given. Now, what page did you say it was? The question is on page 200 of the Joint Appendix, and the answer is on page 201. But all that does is give the witness's name, Mr. Smith. Yes, Justice Sutherland. And where do we find in the record what it is that Mr. Hoth would have said? The first information provided on that was provided back in October of 1981. The letter appears on pages 162 and 163 of the Joint Appendix. This was an attachment to the response to the earlier summary judgment motion, which, along with the decedent's deposition transcript, set out the facts that Hoth did know and was prepared to testify to. The use of this particular Celotex product, Firebar, during that particular time period. When was this filed in the case? This was filed in October of 1981. That is, about two months before the summary judgment motion was made in about three months or four months before Hoth was actually officially listed as a witness. The date of the letter itself is October 15th, and then it was filed on October 19th? Is that what that's significant? Yeah, about right, Your Honor. Where does this letter suggest that there was exposure to asbestos? Let's see. It just says he worked, he worked, oh, in the application, oh, he worked, he supervised and trained crews in the application of Firebar. Is that it? Yes. This letter may not use the word asbestos. Yes, I understand. Now, just a couple more points on the facts. After this second motion came in... Does the letter tell us that there is evidence that Mr. Catrick was exposed to the product as opposed to supervising and training crews? Well, the letter doesn't say anything specific about that, but the product, first of all, was a product that was sprayed into the air, so if you're going to demonstrate it, the asbestos was floating around in the air, and the deposition transcript certainly set out all of that. Yes, they were fireproofing the girders in the buildings when they were doing this, and he would go out and train the crews, and then they would carry on with the product. He was a specialist in this product, which was called Firebar. Now, the response, again, the response to the second summary judgment motion, the one that was dispositive in this case, again included this deposition transcript in the Hoff letter, and it was then a matter of about three weeks later that Hoff was officially listed as a witness. Do you think the deposition transcript helps you much, do you? Only in the sense that it helped to explain the particular facts that were going to be at issue at trial. I certainly don't suggest that that was a separate form of evidence. Indeed, when it was filed, the plaintiff conceded that it was inadmissible under the hearsay rule. I think it's important to understand that there was no suggestion at the time that these three documents, this letter, an additional letter, and the deposition transcript, represented the trial evidence of the plaintiff. They were more illustrative of what she intended to prove, and at all times, the plaintiff made clear that she was going to actually prove these facts through a witness. Now, that's where matters stood when the issue was submitted to the district court, and the question here is whether on these facts, Celotex satisfied its initial obligation to provide some concrete support for its motion. Clearly, I think the answer is no. The only support for the motion was the existing record, and that record, as I've explained, demonstrated that the plaintiff had two uncontested forms of trial evidence available for use. Now, this requirement, that there be some support for a summary judgment motion, is hardly controversial in itself. It is based directly in the language of Rule 56, and has been enforced in a multitude of decisions, most prominently the Atticus decision that was discussed before. I want to make clear that these two recent Court of Appeals cases discussed by Celotex hardly do anything to change the rule. The first, this Matsushita case, the court decided last week, that was a case where both parties had submitted literally a mountain of evidence to the district court prior to the summary judgment ruling, so there could have been no suggestion that the motion by the moving party there was unsupported, in the sense that we had here.
